p1.title: Passage 1
paras: The escalating global water security crisis is often misdiagnosed as a simple challenge of climate-induced scarcity, when it is heavily compounded by systemic mismanagement and misallocated resources. Globally, critical freshwater aquifers are being rapidly depleted by industrial-scale agriculture, driven by inefficient flood irrigation and state-subsidized groundwater extraction. This policy-driven depletion is worsened by widespread industrial pollution and untreated municipal sewage, which turns vital river systems into toxic channels and shrinks the global supply of potable water. Legacy water governance models remain stubbornly centralized, focusing on massive, capital-intensive dams and long-distance water transfer projects that disrupt river ecology and displace marginalized communities. Mitigating this existential threat requires decentralized water governance, centering on localized rainwater harvesting, wastewater recycling, and watershed rejuvenation. Furthermore, agriculture must pivot toward micro-irrigation and crop diversification away from water-intensive cash crops in arid regions. True water security requires treating water not as a commodified, infinite economic input, but as a finite, shared ecological asset that must be protected.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: Science is often presented to the public as a collection of established facts, but its real strength lies in a process: the willingness to test claims, expose them to criticism and discard them when they fail. A single striking study, however elegant, is a beginning rather than a conclusion. Its findings acquire authority only when other researchers, working independently, obtain the same result. In recent years, attempts to repeat well-known experiments in psychology, medicine and other fields have produced unsettling results. A significant proportion of published findings could not be reproduced, or appeared much weaker the second time.

Part of the explanation lies in the incentives under which scientists work. Journals prefer novel and positive results, careers are built on publications, and a study that merely confirms an earlier one rarely attracts attention. Under such pressure, researchers may, often without any intent to deceive, analyse their data in many ways until something appears significant. The remedies now being adopted are instructive: registering a study's methods before data are collected, publishing negative results, and sharing raw data so that others can check the analysis. It would be wrong to conclude from this episode that science is unreliable. The discovery that many findings did not hold up was itself made by scientists, using the methods of science. The crisis is, in this sense, evidence of a system correcting itself.

questions.q: The author says the water crisis is “misdiagnosed” when it is blamed entirely on
opts: inefficient flood irrigation
the absence of large dams
climate-induced scarcity, ignoring systemic mismanagement
decentralised community governance
questions.why: First sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: According to the text, a major policy-driven factor speeding up aquifer depletion is
opts: crop diversification away from cash crops
state-subsidised groundwater extraction and inefficient flood irrigation
nationalising wastewater recycling
mandatory micro-irrigation
questions.why: Second sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: The passage criticises legacy water governance for prioritising
opts: decentralised rainwater harvesting
treating aquifers as protected assets
large, expensive dams and transfer projects that damage river ecology
micro-irrigation subsidies that exclude small farmers
questions.why: Fourth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: To achieve water security, the author says agriculture must
opts: pump more groundwater with power subsidies
move to micro-irrigation and away from water-heavy crops in dry zones
rely only on centralised dams
shift entirely to water-intensive cash crops
questions.why: Sixth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: The final sentence asks society to view water as
opts: an infinite input to be commodified
a secondary resource for industry to manage
an unmanageable asset because of climate
a finite, shared ecological asset that must be protected
questions.why: Last sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

opts: science is fundamentally unreliable and should not be trusted.
a single elegant study is enough to establish a scientific fact.
the failure to reproduce many findings exposes flawed incentives, yet its discovery shows science correcting itself.
journals should publish only novel and positive results.
questions.why: Main idea: incentives explain the problem, but 'The crisis is, in this sense, evidence of a system correcting itself.'

questions.q: Which of the following is mentioned as a remedy now being adopted?
opts: Publishing only positive results.
Keeping raw data confidential.
Rewarding scientists for the number of novel findings.
Registering a study's methods before data are collected.
questions.why: Detail: 'registering a study's methods before data are collected, publishing negative results, and sharing raw data'.

questions.q: The author implies that researchers who analyse their data in many ways until something appears significant:
opts: may produce misleading results even without dishonest intent.
are rarely influenced by career pressures.
produce the most reliable findings.
are always guilty of deliberate fraud.
questions.why: Inference: they do so 'often without any intent to deceive', yet such findings later fail to 'hold up'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards science in the light of these problems is:
opts: dismissive of the problem as trivial.
hostile to the scientists involved.
disillusioned and pessimistic about its future.
confident in its self-correcting process, while acknowledging its flaws.
questions.why: Tone: 'It would be wrong to conclude from this episode that science is unreliable', though the results were 'unsettling'.

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'instructive' means:
opts: confusing and unclear
offering useful lessons
giving orders to others
made compulsory by law
questions.why: Vocabulary: the remedies are 'instructive' because they show what went wrong and how to fix it.
